name: Carthage (Barcid era)

areaKm2.note: Africa ~72,500 km2 (Scullard, https://erenow.org/ancient/a-history-of-the-roman-world-753-to-146-bc/44.php: about 28,000 square miles, directly ruled and tributary land) + Barcid Spain south of the Ebro 120,000-300,000 km2 (educated guess: coastal Andalusia, Murcia, Valencia and the Guadalquivir valley firmly held, the Meseta tribes only as allies) + Ebusus. The historical-basemaps world_bc300 polygon (689,939 km2 measured on the sphere) predates 218: it still shows western Sicily (lost 241) and Sardinia (lost 238) and has only a small Spanish holding, while its African part runs far into the Libyan desert coast; it is used for the map only.

population.note: African territory 3-4 million (Scullard, A History of the Roman World 753-146 BC, ch. VII, https://erenow.org/ancient/a-history-of-the-roman-world-753-to-146-bc/44.php: "an area of about 28,000 square miles and a population of three to four million"; that figure includes the Libyan subjects and Libyphoenician towns) + Barcid Spain 0.5-3 million (educated guess: Andalusia, Murcia and the Levante coast south of the Ebro; no modern count exists). Mid 3.5 + 1.5 million. Western Sicily and Sardinia were lost by 238 BCE and are not counted.

urbanization.note: Carthage city ~250,000 (low end of modern estimates; the Britannica-derived survey at https://warhistory.org/article/pre-roman-north-africa-ii?amp=1 gives ~400,000 incl. slaves and reports Strabo's 700,000 as probably including the Megara suburb and Sahel) + Utica, Hadrumetum, Gades, New Carthage, Hippo and the Libyphoenician towns (~300,000-400,000 together, estimate) = ~0.6-0.7 million of ~5 million.

activePersonnel.note: Sum of the P roles (93,000 / 121,000 / 153,000) and supportPersonnel (20,000 / 28,000 / 40,000), rounded. P roles from Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html) as read by Lazenby and Goldsworthy; see infantry_line. Convention: the mercenary, Libyan, Numidian and Spanish contingents already under arms in spring 218 are counted as active; Spaniards dismissed to their cities in winter 219/218 and discharged veterans are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Polybius 3.35.6 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html): after the Pyrenees Hannibal sent home a number of Spaniards equal to the 10,000 foot and 1,000 horse he left with Hanno, and in winter 219/218 had dismissed the Iberians to their cities (3.33.5) to recall them later. Plus discharged Libyan and Numidian veterans. Range is an estimate.

supportPersonnel.note: Crews: quinqueremes ~300 rowers each (Polybius 1.26.7, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/1*.html, for 256 BCE) x ~87 crewed hulls (32 of the 50 Spanish quinqueremes per Polybius 3.33.14 standard text, + 55 sent against Sicily in 218 per Livy 21.49, https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt) = ~26,000, + trireme crews, engineers, elephant drivers and staff. High allows more hulls crewed in Africa.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Carthage fought with mercenaries, Libyan subjects, Spanish and Numidian allies; citizens served mainly as officers, in the fleet and in emergencies (the citizen levy of 255 and 202). In 215-207 Carthage kept armies in Italy, Spain, Sardinia, Sicily and Africa at once, perhaps 1.5-3x the 218 total.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Libyan heavy infantry, Spanish scutati, Celtiberians, Ligurians. Hannibal's field army line infantry ~72% of his foot (36,000 / 50,000 / 64,000; at the Trebia 20,000 line to 8,000 light per Polybius 3.72) + Spain 12,150 (Libyans, Ligurians) + Africa ~9,000 of the 13,850 Spaniards + 4,000 Metagonians + 0-10,000 garrisons. Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). Spring 218 BCE: (a) Hannibal's field army, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse crossing the Ebro per Polybius 3.35.1, 50,000 foot and 9,000 horse after the Pyrenees (3.35.7); Lazenby thinks the higher figure possible, Goldsworthy treats it as inflated, so low/high span 50,000-90,000 foot; (b) left in Spain with Hasdrubal (3.33.14-16): 11,850 Libyans, 300 Ligurians, 500 Balearians, 450 Libyphoenician and Libyan horse, 300 Ilergetes, 1,800 Numidians, 21 elephants; (c) sent to Africa (3.33.9-13): 1,200 Spanish horse, 13,850 Spanish foot and 870 Balearians (Paton's text runs the last two together; standard reading), plus 4,000 Metagonian foot sent to Carthage; (d) unrecorded garrisons in Libya and the city, 0-10,000 (educated guess).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Libyan infantry well armed (later re-equipped with captured Roman kit); Spanish infantry with the falcata and scutum, era-typical to good.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: long-service mercenaries and subjects hardened by 18 years of Barcid wars in Spain (Polybius 3.35.8 calls the army "highly trained"); Africa garrisons lower.

count.note: Spanish caetrati and Libyan javelinmen: ~25% of Hannibal's foot (12,500 / 18,000 / 23,000) + ~4,850 of the Spaniards sent to Africa (split estimated). Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). Spring 218 BCE: (a) Hannibal's field army, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse crossing the Ebro per Polybius 3.35.1, 50,000 foot and 9,000 horse after the Pyrenees (3.35.7); Lazenby thinks the higher figure possible, Goldsworthy treats it as inflated, so low/high span 50,000-90,000 foot; (b) left in Spain with Hasdrubal (3.33.14-16): 11,850 Libyans, 300 Ligurians, 500 Balearians, 450 Libyphoenician and Libyan horse, 300 Ilergetes, 1,800 Numidians, 21 elephants; (c) sent to Africa (3.33.9-13): 1,200 Spanish horse, 13,850 Spanish foot and 870 Balearians (Paton's text runs the last two together; standard reading), plus 4,000 Metagonian foot sent to Carthage; (d) unrecorded garrisons in Libya and the city, 0-10,000 (educated guess).
Balearic slingers: 500 in Spain + 870 sent to Africa (Polybius 3.33.11, 3.33.16) + 1,500-3,000 with Hannibal (estimate; slingers fought in the 8,000 light screen at the Trebia, Polybius 3.72.7).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Balearic slingers were the era's best slingers.

count.note: Spanish and Libyphoenician close-order horse: ~60-65% of Hannibal's 9,000-12,000 cavalry (split estimated; Hannibal's horse in Italy mixed Spanish and Celtic shock cavalry with Numidians) + 750 Libyphoenicians, Libyans and Ilergetes in Spain + 1,200 Spanish horse sent to Africa. Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). Spring 218 BCE: (a) Hannibal's field army, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse crossing the Ebro per Polybius 3.35.1, 50,000 foot and 9,000 horse after the Pyrenees (3.35.7); Lazenby thinks the higher figure possible, Goldsworthy treats it as inflated, so low/high span 50,000-90,000 foot; (b) left in Spain with Hasdrubal (3.33.14-16): 11,850 Libyans, 300 Ligurians, 500 Balearians, 450 Libyphoenician and Libyan horse, 300 Ilergetes, 1,800 Numidians, 21 elephants; (c) sent to Africa (3.33.9-13): 1,200 Spanish horse, 13,850 Spanish foot and 870 Balearians (Paton's text runs the last two together; standard reading), plus 4,000 Metagonian foot sent to Carthage; (d) unrecorded garrisons in Libya and the city, 0-10,000 (educated guess).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Spanish heavy cavalry outclassed the Roman citizen cavalry at the Ticinus and Cannae.

count.note: Numidian light horse: 3,500-4,000 with Hannibal (estimate from his ~2,000-3,000 surviving Numidians in Italy) + 1,800 Numidians left in Spain (Polybius 3.33.15). Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). Spring 218 BCE: (a) Hannibal's field army, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse crossing the Ebro per Polybius 3.35.1, 50,000 foot and 9,000 horse after the Pyrenees (3.35.7); Lazenby thinks the higher figure possible, Goldsworthy treats it as inflated, so low/high span 50,000-90,000 foot; (b) left in Spain with Hasdrubal (3.33.14-16): 11,850 Libyans, 300 Ligurians, 500 Balearians, 450 Libyphoenician and Libyan horse, 300 Ilergetes, 1,800 Numidians, 21 elephants; (c) sent to Africa (3.33.9-13): 1,200 Spanish horse, 13,850 Spanish foot and 870 Balearians (Paton's text runs the last two together; standard reading), plus 4,000 Metagonian foot sent to Carthage; (d) unrecorded garrisons in Libya and the city, 0-10,000 (educated guess).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Numidian javelin cavalry, the best light horse of the western Mediterranean.

training.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: raised in the saddle, veterans of the Spanish wars.

count.note: 37 elephants crossed the Rhone with Hannibal (Polybius 3.42.11) + 21 left in Spain (3.33.16) = 58 (low) + an unknown number in Africa (Carthage's stables are described by Appian, Pun. 95, for 149 BCE as holding 300; in 215 Carthage sent 40 to Italy, Livy 23.13). Counts animals.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: small North African forest elephants, era-typical.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: trained mahouts; elephants panicked against light troops.

count.note: Quinqueremes and quadriremes: 50 quinqueremes and 2 quadriremes left in Spain (Polybius 3.33.14) + 55 quinqueremes sent against Sicily in 218 (20 + 35, Livy 21.49, https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt). Low counts only the 32 Spanish quinqueremes crewed; high allows hulls in the Carthage harbour (whose ship sheds held 220, https://warhistory.org/article/pre-roman-north-africa-ii?amp=1). Lazenby (isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) stresses how small the Punic navy was compared with 264-241.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Punic quinqueremes were the design Rome copied in 261.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: many hulls laid up after 241; crews short (only 32 of 50 Spanish quinqueremes manned).

count.note: Educated guess: the triremes in Spain (Polybius 3.33.14) plus patrol and dispatch craft in Africa.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 1.0 for Hannibal's own army (best-in-era generalship, Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae) and 0.5 for the Spanish and African commands (Hasdrubal, Hanno); mid 0.75.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5 for a mercenary and multi-ethnic host (Mercenary War 241-237 shows the risk), raised toward 0.75 for the Barcid army bound to its general by long service.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, recent victories (Saguntum 219, conquest of Spain).

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (300 BCE): iron weapons, torsion artillery used at Saguntum 219.

armor.note: Anchor 3: bronze and iron cuirasses, mail for some; many Spanish and Libyan troops lightly armoured.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 (ashlar walls) and above: Carthage's triple land wall and the cothon war harbour; New Carthage fortified.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (depot system) at the low end: Barcid supply bases in Spain, sea supply; few engineered roads.

communications.note: Between anchors 2 (couriers) and 3: couriers and fire signals; no relay-post network documented.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: Numidian scouts, spies in Italy and Gaul before the invasion (Polybius 3.34).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE Tunisia 1,116, Spain 886 (2011 int$). Punic Africa was a rich agricultural and trading economy; Barcid Spain less developed but with large silver mines. Mid 1,000 weights Africa about two-thirds.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: a mercenary state paying for a large standing army in Spain from Spanish silver , while still paying the 1,200-talent indemnity of 241 and Sardinia indemnity of 237; low is the peacetime level.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: shipbuilding, metalworking, purple dye, ceramics, Spanish mining in a mostly agrarian economy.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: fertile Bagradas valley and Sahel estates (Mago's agronomy) exported grain; high relative to the era.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: tracks in the Libyan hinterland and coastal routes in Spain; no engineered road network like Rome's.

majorPorts.note: Carthage, Utica, Hadrumetum, Hippo, New Carthage, Gades, Ebusus, Malaca (count of fleet-capable ports is an estimate).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: the leading western Mediterranean trading power; ~500-1,000 merchantmen of 40-100 t.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or the sea; Hannibal's march from the Ebro to the Po relied on Gallic supplies and foraging.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.06-0.09 horses, mules, oxen and camels per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: Carthage itself was heavily fortified and supplied by sea, but the Libyan subjects revolted in 241-237 and the Spanish dominion was recent; between 1.1 and 1.2.

notes: Snapshot = spring 218 BCE, Hannibal leaving New Carthage at the outbreak of the Second Punic War; forces are the Barcid field army at the start of the march plus the troops left in Spain and Africa. Polybius' figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's Lacinium inscription and are accepted by modern historians; the 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse he gives for the army crossing the Ebro is disputed (Hannibal reached the Po with 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse, Polybius 3.56.4) so the infantry ranges are wide. Population convention: everything ruled from Carthage in 218 (Punic Africa with its Libyan subjects, Barcid Spain, Ebusus); Numidian kingdoms and Iberian allies beyond the Barcid dominion are not counted. Border uses historical-basemaps world_bc300 (nearest file at or before 218), which predates the loss of Sicily (241) and Sardinia (238) and the Barcid conquest of Spain (237-219); areaKm2 is researched separately. Navy numbers are low because the Punic fleet had not been rebuilt after 241.
